summary: Extends the vCard contact format with properties defined by the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) Converged Address Book group. These properties let contact fields that vCard did not already cover be synchronized using OMA Data Synchronization. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: An address book card had no spots for some facts that phones wanted to keep. This memo adds new spots so phones and computers can share the same contact cards.

subtitle: Four new vCard properties and two parameters, borrowed from the OMA Converged Address Book, for hobbies, interests, expertise and directories.

tldr.problem: The Open Mobile Alliance Converged Address Book needs some contact fields that the base vCard specification does not define, and it uses vCard to synchronize contacts between a server and a client.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6715 defines the properties EXPERTISE, HOBBY, INTEREST and ORG-DIRECTORY, plus the parameters INDEX and LEVEL, as vCard extensions, and registers them with IANA.
tldr.outcome: Contact cards can now carry free-form expertise, hobbies, interests and an organization directory link in a standard way, and the document adds no new security considerations beyond the base vCard specification.

facts.label: INDEX values
facts.value: Strictly positive integers; zero not allowed

today: RFC 6715 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the vCard format of RFC 6350.

sections.title: Why These Extensions Exist
sections.content:
Synchronizing an Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) Converged Address Book (CAB) with OMA Data Synchronization commonly uses vCard as the exchange format between the DS Server and the DS Client. The CAB specification defines some contact fields that the base vCard specification, RFC 6350, does not have.

This document reuses the definitions from the OMA-CAB specification and describes them as vCard extensions. It defines the needed properties and parameters, and nothing more.
sections.eli5: Phones and servers swap contact cards to stay in step. Some phone cards had boxes the standard card lacked, so this memo adds those boxes to the standard.

sections.title: The Converged Address Book
sections.content:
The CAB Enabler manages contact information both in user-facing applications and in network-facing activities. At its core is a network-based contact repository where a user stores contacts. Any CAB-enabled device can retrieve them, and the repository can give specific contact information to other users and keep their copies up to date.

It also synchronizes the contacts on the user's devices with the repository, manages the distribution of a user's own information through a Personal Contact Card, and defines a search paradigm so other users can look up people on the system. Its data model is flexible and extensible, covering traditional data such as name, address, email and phone number as well as newer types such as websites, blogs and presence subscription references.
sections.eli5: Think of one big shared address book in the cloud that all your devices copy from. This memo only covers a few extra fields that book uses.

sections.title: The Four New Properties
sections.content:
Four properties are added. Each can appear any number of times and is defined with ABNF, as in RFC 6350.

  • EXPERTISE names a field of expertise. Its LEVEL can be beginner, average or expert.
  • HOBBY names an activity one actively engages in for entertainment, intellectual stimulation, creative expression, or the like. Its LEVEL can be high, medium or low.
  • INTEREST names an activity or topic one finds interesting but does not necessarily engage in. It uses the same three LEVEL values as HOBBY.
  • ORG-DIRECTORY holds a single URI that can be used for an organization-directory lookup, such as finding coworkers or a management chain.

The first three take a single text value. The RFC's examples of the hobby and interest split: "Art" is a hobby if one sculpts or paints, and an interest if one only likes looking at art. "Tennis" is a hobby for someone who plays and an interest for someone who watches.
sections.eli5: There are boxes for what you are good at, what you do for fun, what you just like, and a link to your company's phone book.

sections.title: Free-Form Text and Directory Lookups
sections.content:
EXPERTISE, HOBBY and INTEREST are intended as free-form naming, meant for human consumption. No specific lists of allowed strings are defined. The RFC expects that de facto taxonomies might develop: one vCard may say "philately", another "stamp collecting" and a third "old postage stamps". Usage, not specification, may favor one term over time. These values are not meant for automated categorization that would need standard terms and registries.

ORG-DIRECTORY works differently because its value is a URI. How the lookup is done depends on the URI scheme, and the RFC does not specify the lookup mechanism. An HTTP URI might lead to a web form meant for manual use in a browser, so it might not be usable for automated searching. The entity the vCard describes would presumably be found in the directory, but that is not required.
sections.eli5: You can write anything you like in the hobby box, like "stamp collecting" or "old postage stamps". People will probably settle on favorite words over time.

sections.title: The INDEX and LEVEL Parameters
sections.content:
INDEX is used in a multi-valued property to show the position of a value within the set. It takes an integer, and values must be strictly positive: zero is not allowed. The properties above all accept it.

LEVEL shows the level of expertise, hobby or interest attained. The allowed values depend on the property: beginner, average or expert with EXPERTISE, and high, medium or low with HOBBY or INTEREST.

The property definitions also allow the usual vCard parameters, such as language, pref, altid and type.
sections.eli5: INDEX says which one is first, second or third on your list. LEVEL says how good you are, or how much you like it.

sections.title: What the Lines Look Like
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples in vCard line syntax. A person who is an expert in chemistry and a beginner in Chinese literature, with two hobbies and two directory links, could have lines like these:

  • EXPERTISE;INDEX=1;LEVEL=expert:chemistry
  • HOBBY;INDEX=1;LEVEL=high:reading
  • INTEREST;INDEX=1;LEVEL=medium:r&b music
  • ORG-DIRECTORY;INDEX=1:http://directory.mycompany.example.com

A directory can also be an LDAP URI, as in ORG-DIRECTORY;PREF=1:ldap://ldap.tech.example/o=Example%20Tech,ou=Engineering.
sections.eli5: Each fact goes on its own line, like "hobby, number one, a lot: reading".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 6715 presents no security considerations beyond those in Section 9 of the base vCard specification, RFC 6350.
sections.eli5: These new boxes add no new safety worries beyond the ones the normal contact card already has.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added entries to three registries defined in RFC 6350: the vCard Properties registry, the vCard Parameters registry and the vCard Parameter Values registry. The property entries cover EXPERTISE, HOBBY and INTEREST, the parameter entries cover INDEX and LEVEL, and the parameter-value entries list each allowed LEVEL value for the property it applies to.

One oddity: the property table in the IANA section names the fourth property ORG-URI and points to Section 2.4, while Section 2.4 itself defines ORG-DIRECTORY. The INDEX examples in Section 3.1 also use ORG-URI. The RFC text does not explain the difference.
sections.eli5: The official list of allowed card fields was updated to include the new ones. The list uses a slightly different name for the directory field than the rest of the memo does.
